newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo ferrous metals sector sees record 1996 growth.
newsitem.headline: Yugo ferrous metals sector sees record 1996 growth.

text.p: Yugoslavia's ferrous metals sector hopes to get back on its feet and restore pre-war production levels by the end of 1997 despite daunting odds that include a diminished local market and tougher competition abroad.
Yugoslavia's pig iron output in the January-October period reached 415,000 tonnes, or some 308 percent more than in the same ten-month period 1995, the Yugoslav ferrous metallurgy association said.
Raw steel output rose to 518,000 tonnes, or by around 223 percent against last year's figure, Arsenije Jovanovic, director of the association, told Reuters.
Commodity (finished and semi-finished goods) production stood at 538,000 tonnes, an increase of 160 percent on the same period last year.

The ferrous metals industry topped the industrial growth list in 1996, with output in October 162.4 percent up against the same month last year. Cumulative ten month production was 164.1 percent above the same period in 1995.

By the year end, total production of pig iron was expected to reach 565,000 tonnes, or 324 percent more than last year, while raw steel output was estimated at some 695,000 tonnes, or 282 percent up on 1995.
On the basis of these estimates, Jovanovic said production of commodity goods by year end was expected to reach around 680,000 tonnes, or 170 percent more than last year.
Of total commodity output, around 335,000 tonnes would be earmarked for export.

The association forecast 20 percent growth in the metal processing sector in 1997, with growing domestic demand for iron and steel products and normalisation of Yugoslavia's relations with international organisations and markets.
Overall output of the ferrous metals industry would increase between 60 and 65 percent next year compared to 1996, bringing iron and steel production close to the record 1989 levels, Jovanovic said.
Commodity production was expected to reach 1.2 million tonnes, or 75 percent more than this year.
This will still be below the level before the breakup of the former Yugoslav federation in 1991, since there are not as many deals for processing customer supplied goods now, Jovanovic said.
"Despite this, the ferrous metals sector is one of the first industrial branches which will return to pre-war level of operation in normal conditions," he added.
Nearly 300,000 tonnes of commodity production would go for further processing while some 380,000 tonnes would be sold on the domestic market.
"We will have to export around 500,000 to 600,000 tonnes or more than 50 percent of output," Jovanovic said.
The association has called for measures to cut steel imports "under precisely established quotas".
It said imports of steel at dumping prices, primarily from east European countries, were hurting domestic producers.

Loss of foreign markets due to three and a half years of sanctions against rump Yugoslavia, comprising Serbia and Montenegro, and a shrunken domestic market after the breakup of former Yugoslavia, brought the Yugoslav ferrous metals industry to a virtual standstill.
"Returning to world markets will be a hard and long process requiring better technological performance that many of our producers are not yet able to meet," Jovanovic said.
Exports from Serbia and Montenegro in the last few years before the former federation's breakup in 1991 stood at between 600,000 and 800,000 tonnes per year.
"We will probably have to target the same volume of exports in the next few years until our local market is revived, since our capacities are much bigger," Jovanovic said.
"But we cannot reduce or adjust our production, that would be irrational. We cannot go half-way."
Yugoslavia's ferrous metallurgy industry employs around 17,000 people, 12,500 of which work in the two biggest steel works in Smederevo and Niksic. -- Amra Kevic, Belgrade newsroom +381 11 2224305
